source.title: Case Study 14: Thrown from a Galloping Horse

classification.acuity_basis: Shock-like vitals resolved over 1h, focused spine assessment cleared, negative orthostatic test; patient walked out next day.

context.distance_to_care: long way from trailhead; help likely not before dark or next morning

presentation.summary: Rider thrown from a stumbling horse lands on her back, tumbles, stands, runs a few steps and collapses. Bystanders reach her within a minute. She is alert, anxious, in pain, breathing fast but unlabored, with a strong fast radial pulse.
presentation.chief_complaint: right upper back and shoulder pain
exam_findings: 6x6 inch abrasion over right scapula, no point tenderness, no active bleeding
presentation.last_intake_output: normal urine and BM today; lunch, ~2 L water plus tea
presentation.events_leading_up: no dizziness or symptoms before the fall

plan: log roll onto pad and into sleeping bag, legs elevated ~8 in
calm patient, oral water, serial vitals
reassess for missed internal injury
clean and dress abrasion
focused spine assessment to decide on spine protection
make an evacuation plan
teaching_points: Walking after the event does not rule out spine injury; stress response lets people move despite injury.
Shock signs without an obvious injury raise concern for internal injury.
Acute stress response mimics shock but should settle over serial vitals in a healthy uninjured person.
Orthostatic check: supine then stand 1 min; HR rise >=30/min in adults, dizziness or fainting is positive. Symptoms matter more than numbers.

decision_points.question: Can spine protection be released?
basis: no spine pain or tenderness on repeat palpation

outcome.summary: Vitals normalized; walked to camp; only complaint sore abraded shoulder; planned to walk out next day.
outcome.final_diagnosis: abrasion, acute stress response; no major injury

must_ask: numbness or tingling in arms or legs?
eval.must_escalate: Plan evacuation if shock signs persist or worsen, or spine cannot be cleared.
must_not_recommend: clearing the spine just because she walked
having her stand before reassessing vitals and spine

lay_queries: my friend got thrown off a horse and landed on her back
she fell off a horse and got up but now she's pale and sweaty
fell off horse shoulder hurts can she walk
red_flags: pale cool clammy skin with fast weak pulse

title: Rider on a pale horse (wind knocked out)

source.title: Case Study 37: Rider on a Pale Horse

classification.acuity_basis: Vitals normalized in 30 min; spine cleared; walked out and was driven to ER, released.

presentation.summary: Rider ejected from a bucking horse lands on their back, stands, walks several steps and kneels, gasping. Airway open, no chest injury found, radial pulse present. Patient gasps that the wind was knocked out; breathing settles in a minute or two.
presentation.chief_complaint: right upper back and shoulder pain
exam_findings: 6x6 inch bruise over right scapula, no point tenderness
presentation.last_intake_output: normal urine/BM; lunch, 2 L water plus tea

plan: on pad, insulated, legs elevated ~8 in with knees bent
oral water
packs as soft head blocks to limit neck motion
serial vitals
focused spine assessment
evacuation plan
anticipated_problems: evacuation support needed if spine protection continues
teaching_points: Shock vs acute stress response: stress response should settle with time.
Positional vitals: stand, wait 1 min; HR rise >=30 or dizziness/fainting suggests shock.
Soft head blocks are enough; cervical collar unnecessary, a soft rolled collar acceptable.

outcome.summary: Slow walk to trailhead, driven to ER, cleared and released.

must_recognize: wind knocked out vs true respiratory compromise
eval.must_escalate: Evacuate if vitals do not normalize or abdominal/chest signs develop.

lay_queries: someone fell off a horse and can't catch their breath
got the wind knocked out of him and now he's really pale

title: Fall from a tree onto upper back at a campground

classification.acuity_basis: Thoracic spine pain and tenderness after significant fall; EMS called and transported.

context.region: established campground a few miles from town

presentation.summary: Companion falls about 15 ft from a tree when a branch snaps while hanging a bear bag, landing on his upper back. Rescuer immediately takes manual c-spine control.
presentation.chief_complaint: right shoulder and upper back pain
exam_findings: pain on the spine and paraspinal muscles
tenderness on spine between shoulder blades
presentation.last_intake_output: 4 L water, urinated twice, normal BM

assessment: possible spine injury (mechanism plus thoracic pain and tenderness)
plan: maintain spine protection: log roll onto pad, improvised rolled-jacket collar, soft head blocks
call 911
anticipated_problems: if EMS can't come, prepare for a night in the field
teaching_points: Spine pain or tenderness means a focused spine assessment cannot clear the spine.
Practice is moving from rigid 'immobilization' to 'spine protection' with careful handling.
Hard collars restrict imperfectly and can interfere with airway; soft or improvised collars serve as reminders.
Backboards are extrication tools; prolonged use causes pain and pressure sores. Supine on a firm surface is the standard; vacuum mattress preferred for remote carries per WMS/ICAR.

decision_points.question: Can the spine be cleared in the field?

outcome.summary: EMS confirmed findings, swapped to commercial soft collar, lifted onto cot with straps and head blocks (no backboard), transported.

must_recognize: spine tenderness after a significant fall cannot be cleared in the field
must_ask: does pressing on the spine hurt?
eval.must_escalate: Call EMS; keep patient still on a firm surface.

lay_queries: my buddy fell out of a tree onto his back
fell 15 feet back hurts between shoulder blades
red_flags: midline spine tenderness after fall from height

title: Teen tumbles 40 ft downhill during bear encounter

classification.acuity_basis: Spine cleared by focused assessment; abrasions treated; patient continued hiking.

context.region: ridge on east border of Yellowstone NP

presentation.summary: A black bear on the trail startles the group; a student steps off the trail and rolls about 40 ft downhill with a 40 lb pack, stopped by a tree. Responder confirms scene safety and has another student hold spine control.
exam_findings: multiple small abrasions knees and forearms
large abrasion back of right thigh
presentation.last_intake_output: breakfast, lunch, 3 L water, clear urine

plan: confirm bear is gone
move patient back to trail
irrigate and clean abrasions, dress worst with antibiotic ointment gauze
focused spine assessment
teaching_points: Scene safety first even in an emergency.
Selective spine protocols based on signs and symptoms are endorsed by NAEMSP, WMS, ICAR and others.

decision_points.question: Release spine control?
basis: no spine pain/tenderness on full palpation

outcome.summary: Hiked out with group; stopped at stream to rehydrate and clean wounds; no further problems.

must_recognize: tumbling fall is a spine mechanism
must_ask: did he hit his head or black out?
must_not_recommend: approaching before the animal threat is gone

we saw a bear and someone fell down the slope

title: Achy elbow after skiing turns out to be spreading infection

classification.acuity_basis: Spreading infection with fever = systemic; needs physician and antibiotics; later required IV antibiotics and drainage.

pertinent_history: recurrent eczema-like skin bumps; small lesions on elbow the week before
medications: ibuprofen 400 mg q4-6h since previous morning

presentation.summary: After two days of hard skiing, a 40-year-old develops a painful, red, swollen elbow with limited motion. He attributes it to bursitis from overuse. By the next day his resting heart rate is up and he has a low fever.
presentation.chief_complaint: dull aching left elbow pain, 5-6/10, spikes to 9 when bumped
exam_findings: swelling extends several inches above and below elbow
presentation.last_intake_output: well hydrated, good appetite, normal output

vitals.note: HR high for this patient (baseline 50-60); 100F oral

plan: see a physician next morning (no local hospital)
in the backcountry: evacuate for physician evaluation and possible antibiotics
teaching_points: Cardinal signs of soft tissue infection: redness, swelling, warmth, pain; also red streaks, fever, chills, swollen nodes, pus.
Redness and fever are inconsistent with a simple strain.
Mark the edge of redness with a pen to track spread over 18-24 h.
Warm soaks every 1-2 h, elevation and immobilization help.
Expedite evacuation if no improvement 24-36 h after starting antibiotics or with systemic signs.

outcome.summary: Oral antibiotics failed; ED admission for IV clindamycin, bursa drained; full recovery in 21 days.

must_recognize: signs of spreading soft tissue infection
must_ask: any cuts, bites or skin lesions nearby?
eval.must_escalate: Seek physician within 24 h; evacuate from backcountry.
must_not_recommend: treating as a simple strain and continuing activity

lay_queries: my elbow is red and swollen and hot after skiing
swollen elbow and I have a low fever

title: Rider falls from rearing horse onto head

classification.acuity_basis: Brief altered responsiveness, headache, vomiting; near road; SAR evacuated, ER observation overnight.

presentation.summary: A horse rears and the rider falls backward onto his head and left shoulder. He is initially responsive only to voice (moaning), becoming fully oriented within 1-2 minutes.
presentation.last_intake_output: 1 L water, breakfast, normal BM, vomited once after fall

plan: spine protection: log roll onto pad, improvised collar, head blocks
monitor for worsening head injury, vomiting, mental status changes
RICE shoulder
call local EMS/SAR and support evacuation
anticipated_problems: signs of serious head injury requiring rapid evacuation
teaching_points: Near a road, defer to local EMS/SAR rather than wilderness spine clearance protocols.
Mild head injury: brief LOR change, headache, nausea, vomiting; monitor and periodically wake.
Serious head injury: airway care, head elevated 6-8 in, rapid evacuation.

decision_points.question: Use wilderness spine clearance?
decision_points.source_decision: No; hand off to local SAR because road was close

outcome.summary: SAR evacuated by wheeled litter with spine precautions; vomited once more; ER found no spine injury, kept overnight for mild head injury.

must_ask: was he knocked out or confused?
how many times has he vomited?
eval.must_escalate: Activate EMS/SAR; rapid evacuation if mental status worsens.

lay_queries: he fell off a horse on his head and was out of it for a minute
hit his head and threw up

title: Lead climbing fall with ankle injury and thigh laceration

classification.acuity_basis: Ankle usable (weight bearing), wound closable; trip continued.

context.region: desert, car camping in National Forest
context.distance_to_care: 30 min dirt road to highway + 1 h to town

pertinent_history: peanut allergy, one severe reaction years ago

presentation.summary: Leader falls about 12 ft and swings into the rock feet first, grabbing his right ankle. Wearing a helmet; did not hit head. Lowered to a ledge.
exam_findings: 2 in x 1/4 in laceration right lateral mid-thigh
right ankle swollen, general tenderness, no point tenderness
pertinent_negatives: no head, neck or back pain

plan: usability test: patient can bear weight
direct pressure for minor bleeding
in camp: irrigate, clean, dress abrasion; close non-gaping clean laceration with strips
RICE ankle; tape for support
teaching_points: Don't grade sprains in the field; decide usable vs unusable. Usable -> RICE/tape; unusable -> immobilize and evacuate.
RICE: rest, ice 20-40 min every 2-4 h for 24-48 h, compression, elevation.
Lacerations wider than ~1/2 in should be packed open and seen by a physician.
Wound cleaning: hand hygiene, gloves, pressure irrigation with disinfected water, remove debris, dress, recheck CSM; watch for redness, swelling, pus, heat, pain.

outcome.summary: Wounds healed; ankle managed with RICE and daytime tape; trip continued.

must_ask: can you put weight on it?
is there one exact spot that hurts when pressed?
can you feel and wiggle your toes?
eval.must_escalate: Immobilize and evacuate if unable to bear weight.
must_not_recommend: closing a gaping, dirty, or wide wound in the field

lay_queries: I fell climbing and twisted my ankle
cut on my thigh should I close it

title: BASE jumping accident: partial amputation, open fractures, hemorrhagic shock

classification.acuity_basis: Ongoing hemorrhage despite tourniquet, falling BP; air evacuation.

context.distance_to_care: hours; needs litter lower to helicopter landing zone

pertinent_history: prior open fracture left leg 3 years ago

presentation.summary: Jumper's chute opened facing the wall; he struck the cliff and the ground at high speed. Found in blood-soaked sand on a steep talus slope with rockfall risk, helmet on, an improvised tourniquet already applied and still bleeding.
exam_findings: right leg partial below-knee amputation (~10% attached), active bleeding through improvised tourniquet
deformed closed right ankle fracture; foot cold, pulseless, numb but toes move
left open lower leg fracture with large exposed tissue
left shoulder and wrist tenderness without deformity
presentation.last_intake_output: energy bars, ~2 L water in 6 h; multiple vomits

vitals.note: bleeding resumed through tourniquet; second tourniquet applied above

assessment: hypovolemic shock from hemorrhage and vomiting
possible left humerus, clavicle, scapula, wrist fractures
plan: make scene safe from rockfall; reroute rescuers
control hemorrhage: pressure dressing failed, commercial tourniquet placed above knee
manual spine stabilization
request ALS, litter team, high-angle gear via incident command
remove harness, dress wounds, splint fractures
frequent vitals
package in litter and lower toward helicopter LZ
teaching_points: Tourniquets can lose effectiveness over time; reassess and add a second above the first if bleeding resumes.
Wilderness rescues change; revisit scene safety and evacuation plans as patient and terrain evolve.
Patient assessment system is iterative.

decision_points.question: Continue nighttime lowering?
decision_points.source_decision: No; stop and hold for dawn helicopter hoist

outcome.summary: Survived the night; hoisted at dawn then flown to trauma center. Right leg amputated below knee; 1 week ICU.
outcome.final_diagnosis: traumatic below-knee amputation R, L tib/fib fracture, L clavicle and wrist fractures

must_ask: is the tourniquet tight and above the wound?
eval.must_escalate: Immediate SAR/EMS and air evacuation; hemorrhage control first.
must_not_recommend: delaying hemorrhage control for spine care
giving large amounts of oral fluid to a vomiting shocked patient

lay_queries: his leg is almost cut off and won't stop bleeding
tourniquet isn't working blood still coming
base jumper hit the cliff

title: Teen camper hits head on log, possible concussion with hyperventilation

source.title: Case Study: A Blow to the Head

classification.acuity_basis: Mild head injury S/S, A+Ox4; walked to road and clinic evaluation same day.

context.distance_to_care: 2 mi walk to parking, then drive to clinic

presentation.summary: Camper tripped an hour earlier and struck his forehead on a log. Peers say he was 'knocked out' for a few minutes; he says he was stunned but remembers it. Arrives breathing very fast; takes 20 minutes of coaching to slow.
presentation.last_intake_output: breakfast, snacks, 2 L electrolyte water, normal urine/BM

assessment: low-risk spine mechanism; walked a mile; meets criteria for no spine protection
plan: calm patient, coach slow breathing
monitor for worsening head injury
walk without pack 2 mi to parking, drive to clinic
stop and call for help if worsening
teaching_points: A fall from standing height is not a spinal cord injury mechanism.
Hyperventilation causes hand pain, tingling, cramping; resolves with slowed breathing.
If unsure about loss of responsiveness, decide based on current mental status.
Mild head injury S/S: brief LOR change, seeing stars, nausea or isolated vomiting, headache, dizziness, lethargy, amnesia.
Worsening S/S: worsening headache, vision change, persistent vomiting, excessive sleepiness, ataxia, seizure, disorientation/combativeness, slowing bounding pulse, erratic breathing, unequal pupils.
Observe 24 h if A+Ox3-4 with only mild S/S. Evacuate if any LOR loss or altered mental status, or no improvement at 24 h. Rapid evac if not A+Ox3-4, mental status changes, or serious S/S.

decision_points.question: Evacuate or monitor?
decision_points.source_decision: Walk out to road and clinic with fallback to call for help

outcome.summary: Stable during walk; clinic diagnosed possible concussion; referred to family physician.

eval.must_escalate: Rapid evacuation if mental status changes or serious head injury signs appear.
must_not_recommend: spine immobilization for a standing-height fall with normal exam

lay_queries: kid hit his head on a log and his friends say he blacked out
he's breathing really fast and his hands hurt after hitting his head

title: Missing snowmobiler: crash, mild hypothermia, head injury

classification.acuity_basis: Altered mental status, unknown down time, cold exposure; EMS transport.

context.weather: winter storm warning, blowing snow, visibility <20 m

pertinent_history: cardiac risk factors, no prior MI

presentation.summary: Overdue experienced snowmobiler found beside a damaged machine that hit a tree, in a blizzard. Responds only to loud voice, chest skin cool, breathing, carotid pulse present, no obvious injury on rapid check. Scene judged unsafe; patient wrapped tarp-bag-tarp and sledded to EMS with manual head contact.
symptoms: amnesia for the crash and the day
exam_findings: hands and feet cold but soft and pliable, rewarm pink with good CSM

assessment: mild hypothermia (shivering, mental status, measured temperature)
mechanism for spine injury; cannot do focused spine assessment
plan: unsafe scene: package quickly (tarp, sleeping bag, tarp) and move
manual spine protection during transport
in ambulance: remove wet clothing, warm blankets, soft collar, supine on cot
teaching_points: When the scene is unsafe, package and move before full assessment.
Inner tarp keeps the sleeping bag dry and insulating.
Modern 'spine protection' replaces rigid immobilization; hands-on c-spine protection was within standard of care.

outcome.summary: Mild hypothermia resolved within an hour in warm ambulance/ER. Concussion, no spine injury.

must_ask: do you have dry insulation and a vapor barrier?
eval.must_escalate: Get to EMS; hypothermia plus altered mental status after crash needs transport.
must_not_recommend: staying in the storm to complete a full exam

lay_queries: found him in the snow by his snowmobile and he's barely answering
he's freezing and confused after crashing
